exercises.prompt: In Buenos Aires, how does a friend say *you have* to you, using *vos*?

options.label: vos tenés
options.feedback: Yes. Voseo forms are stressed on the ending, so there's no stem change: *tenés*.

options.label: vos tienes
options.feedback: Not quite — that mixes the pronoun *vos* with the *tú* verb form; in Buenos Aires the verb is *tenés*.

options.label: vos tenéis
options.feedback: Not yet — *tenéis* is the *vosotros* form used in Spain.

options.label: vos tiene
options.feedback: Not yet — *tiene* is the *usted* (or *él/ella*) form.

hints: Voseo forms of the present are stressed on the last syllable.
Take *tener*, drop the *-r*, add *-s*, and put the stress on the ending.
exercises.solution: In the voseo of the Río de la Plata, the present is formed from the infinitive with the stress on the ending: *tener → **tenés***. Because the stress isn't on the stem, there is no *e → ie* change (compare *tú tienes*).

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap with the voseo form of *ser*: *Vos ___ muy amable.*
hints: *Ser* is irregular in the voseo too.
It's a three-letter word.
exercises.solution: The voseo form of *ser* is irregular: ***sos*** (compare *tú eres*). *Vos **sos** muy amable* = You're very kind.

feedback.message: That's the *vosotros* form used in Spain. With *vos*: *sos*.

exercises.prompt: Fill the gap with the *vosotros* form of *querer*: *¿Vosotros ___ café o té?*
hints: *Vosotros* forms end in *-áis, -éis, -ís*.
There's no stem change in the *vosotros* form.
exercises.solution: *Vosotros* forms of *-er* verbs end in **-éis**, and, as with *nosotros*, there is no stem change: *querer → **queréis***. *¿Vosotros **queréis** café o té?*

feedback.message: Almost — the *vosotros* form has no stem change: *queréis*.
Almost — *queréis* needs its accent on the *é*.
That's the *ustedes* form, which is perfect in Latin America. The prompt asks for *vosotros*: *queréis*.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the question as it would be asked in Latin America, with *ustedes*: *¿Vosotros venís mañana?*
hints: *Ustedes* takes the third person plural verb.
*Venir* → *vienen*.
exercises.solution: *Ustedes* is grammatically third person plural, so *venís* becomes ***vienen***: *¿Ustedes vienen mañana?* (or simply *¿Vienen mañana?*). In Spain this would sound formal; in Latin America it's the normal informal plural.

feedback.message: Almost — *ustedes* takes a third person plural verb: *vienen*.

exercises.prompt: In Buenos Aires, what is the most usual word for *car*?

options.label: auto
options.feedback: Yes. *Auto* is the usual word in Argentina, Chile and Uruguay.

options.label: coche
options.feedback: Not quite — *coche* is the usual word in Spain (and is understood elsewhere).

options.label: carro
options.feedback: Not quite — *carro* is usual in Mexico, Central America, Colombia, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

options.label: camión
options.feedback: Not yet — *camión* means truck in most places, and bus in Mexico.

hints: Think of the Southern Cone.
It's also short for *automóvil*.
exercises.solution: In Argentina, Chile and Uruguay the everyday word is ***auto***. Spain says *coche*; Mexico, Central America, Colombia, Venezuela and the Caribbean say *carro*. All three are understood everywhere.

exercises.prompt: Where do *casa* (house) and *caza* (hunt) normally sound exactly the same?

options.label: In Latin America, the Canary Islands and parts of Andalusia
options.feedback: Yes. That's seseo, used by the great majority of Spanish speakers in the world.

options.label: Only in Madrid
options.feedback: Not yet — most of Spain, including Madrid, has distinción: *caza* with a *th* sound.

options.label: Nowhere: they are always pronounced differently
options.feedback: Not yet — in seseo areas they are pronounced identically.

options.label: Only in written Spanish
options.feedback: Not yet — in writing they are always different (*s* versus *z*). The question is about pronunciation.

hints: Which phenomenon makes *s*, *z* and *c* (before *e, i*) sound the same?
It's the majority pronunciation worldwide.
exercises.solution: In **seseo** areas, all of Latin America, the Canary Islands and parts of Andalusia, *z* and *c* (before *e, i*) sound like *s*, so *casa* and *caza* are homophones. Most of Spain uses **distinción**, where *caza* has a *th* sound.

exercises.prompt: Which of these sentences are accepted as standard by the Spanish academies? Choose all that apply.

options.label: A Juan lo vi ayer.
options.feedback: Yes. The standard direct object pronoun for a man.

options.label: A Juan le vi ayer.
options.feedback: Yes. Leísmo with a masculine singular person is accepted; it's common in Spain.

options.label: A María le vi ayer.
options.feedback: Not yet — with a woman as direct object, the standard pronoun is *la*: *A María la vi*.

options.label: El libro le compré ayer.
options.feedback: Not yet — with a thing, the direct object pronoun must be *lo*: *El libro lo compré ayer*.

hints: The standard direct object pronouns are *lo, la*.
Leísmo is accepted only in one specific case.
exercises.solution: **a** is the general standard. **b** is leísmo with a masculine singular person, accepted by the academies and common in central and northern Spain. **c** (*le* for a woman) and **d** (*le* for a thing) are not standard; use *la* and *lo*.

exercises.prompt: Give the voseo command of *venir*: *¡___ acá, que te quiero mostrar algo!*
hints: Voseo commands are formed from the infinitive by dropping the *-r*.
The stress stays on the last syllable, so it needs an accent.
exercises.solution: Voseo commands drop the final *-r* of the infinitive and keep the stress on the last syllable: *venir → **vení***. *¡Vení acá, que te quiero mostrar algo!* Compare *tú*: *¡Ven aquí!*

feedback.message: That's the *tú* command. With *vos*, drop the *-r* of the infinitive: *vení*.
Almost — the voseo command is stressed on the last syllable, so it's written *vení*.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish as it would be said in Spain, to two friends: *Can you help me?*
hints: In Spain, the informal plural is *vosotros*.
*Poder* → *podéis*, then *ayudarme* (or *me podéis ayudar*).
exercises.solution: In Spain, talking to two friends, you use **vosotros**: *poder → **podéis***. The object pronoun can go on the infinitive or before *podéis*: ***¿Podéis ayudarme?*** or ***¿Me podéis ayudar?*** In Latin America you'd say *¿Pueden ayudarme?*

feedback.message: Perfect in Latin America (and formal in Spain). For friends in Spain, use *vosotros*: *¿podéis ayudarme?*

exercises.prompt: Which statement best describes the Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española (ASALE)?

options.label: It brings together the Spanish language academies of many countries, which prepare the dictionary, grammar and spelling rules jointly.
options.feedback: Yes. Since its foundation in 1951 it has grown into a network of more than twenty academies working on shared reference works.

options.label: It is a department of the Spanish government that decides how people in Latin America should speak.
options.feedback: Not yet — ASALE isn't a government body, and its policy treats each country's educated usage as equally valid.

options.label: It certifies learners' level of Spanish with official exams.
options.feedback: Not yet — that's the Instituto Cervantes, with the DELE and SIELE exams.

options.label: It was founded in 1713 in Madrid.
options.feedback: Not yet — 1713 and Madrid are the foundation of the Real Academia Española. ASALE was founded in Mexico in 1951.

hints: Reread the culture section.
Think "association" of academies.
exercises.solution: **ASALE** is the association of the Spanish language academies, founded in Mexico in 1951. Its members, including the RAE, prepare the *Diccionario de la lengua española*, the grammar and the spelling rules together, under a panhispanic policy that recognises the educated usage of every country. The RAE itself was founded in Madrid in 1713.

exercises.prompt: What is the usual word for *computer* in Spain?
hints: It's different from most of Latin America.
It comes from French *ordinateur*.
exercises.solution: In Spain a computer is an ***ordenador*** (a word borrowed from French *ordinateur*). Most of Latin America says *computadora*, and Chile and Colombia often *computador*.

feedback.message: That's the usual word in most of Latin America. In Spain: *ordenador*.
